questions.stem: According to the Big Bang theory, approximately how old is the universe?

options.text: 1 billion years
100 billion years
4.6 billion years
13.8 billion years

questions.explanation: The Big Bang theory states that the universe began approximately 13.8 billion years ago. This age is determined from multiple independent methods including the Hubble constant and analysis of the cosmic microwave background.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the Big Bang?

options.text: An explosion at a single point in pre-existing space
A collision between two galaxies
A chemical reaction that created all the elements
The expansion of space itself from an extremely hot, dense state, with no centre

questions.explanation: The Big Bang was not an explosion at a point in space. Instead, space itself was created and expanded from an extremely hot, dense state. There is no centre to the universe because the Big Bang happened everywhere simultaneously.

questions.stem: What is the cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation?

options.text: The cooled afterglow of the early universe, detected as microwaves at about 2.7 K from all directions
Radiation from mobile phone masts
Background radiation from radioactive rocks on Earth
Microwave radiation from the Sun

questions.explanation: The CMB is uniform microwave radiation at 2.7 K detected from all directions. It was released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang when atoms first formed, and has been red shifted from gamma radiation to microwaves by the expansion of space.

questions.stem: Why is the CMB radiation in the microwave range rather than the gamma ray range?

options.text: Because microwaves travel faster than gamma rays
Because the Big Bang only produced low-energy radiation
Because the expansion of the universe has stretched the wavelength of the original radiation by about 1000 times
Because gamma rays are absorbed by space dust

questions.explanation: The CMB was originally emitted as high-energy radiation when the universe was about 3000 K. The expansion of the universe has stretched the wavelength of this radiation by about 1000 times, shifting it from the gamma/visible range into the microwave range.

questions.stem: How does the red shift of galaxies support the Big Bang theory?

options.text: It shows that galaxies are getting hotter over time
It shows that all galaxies are moving towards us
It shows the universe is expanding, implying everything was once much closer together
It shows that galaxies are all the same age

questions.explanation: Red shift shows that distant galaxies are all moving away from us and that more distant galaxies recede faster. If we extrapolate backward, everything was once concentrated together, supporting the idea of a single origin event — the Big Bang.

questions.stem: Which observation about the abundance of elements supports the Big Bang theory?

options.text: Heavier elements are more abundant than lighter ones
All elements were created in equal amounts
The universe is about 75% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass, matching Big Bang nucleosynthesis predictions
The universe contains mostly iron and carbon

questions.explanation: The observed ratio of about 75% hydrogen and 25% helium matches the predictions for nuclear reactions occurring in the first few minutes after the Big Bang. There is far too much helium for it to have been produced by stellar fusion alone.

questions.stem: Who discovered the cosmic microwave background radiation?

options.text: Albert Einstein
Edwin Hubble
Isaac Newton
Penzias and Wilson

questions.explanation: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson discovered the cosmic microwave background radiation accidentally in 1965 at Bell Labs. They detected an unexplained microwave noise coming uniformly from all directions, which was later identified as the predicted afterglow of the Big Bang.
